title: Workations: How to Travel Without Torching Your Career
metaDescription: A practical guide to working remotely while travelling — time zones, connectivity, tax and legal issues, and how to structure a workation that actually works.
excerpt: Working from a beach is a terrible idea. Working from a town near a beach, on a schedule you designed, is a very good one.
author: Travel Editors
content:
The stock photograph shows a laptop on a beach towel. Anyone who has tried it knows the screen is unreadable, the sand gets everywhere, and the battery dies in ninety minutes.

A **workation** done properly looks nothing like that. It looks like an ordinary working week in a place where the evenings and weekends are better, and the difference between the two versions is almost entirely planning.

## Be Honest About Which Version You Are Doing

Three distinct things get called the same name, and conflating them is the root of most disappointment:

- **A working trip** — full hours, normal output, different location. The weekends and evenings are the holiday.
- **A reduced-hours trip** — agreed part-time or flexible hours, genuinely less output, more exploring.
- **A holiday with some work in it** — mostly leisure, a couple of hours a day, checking in rather than delivering.

Decide which one you are doing, tell your employer or clients, and plan accordingly. Most workation misery comes from attempting the third while having promised the first.

## The Time Zone Question Comes First

Before the destination, before the accommodation, before anything: **what hours will you actually work?**

- **Within 3 hours of home** — barely an adjustment. The easiest and most sustainable option.
- **4 to 6 hours ahead** — you work afternoon and evening, mornings are free. This is the best-structured version of a workation: you explore while everyone else is asleep, then work. Europe from India, or Asia from Europe, both work this way.
- **4 to 6 hours behind** — you start very early and finish mid-afternoon. Harder, but it leaves good afternoons.
- **8+ hours difference** — you are working nights. Some people manage it for a week. Almost nobody manages it for a month without their health and work quality degrading.

A common mistake is choosing the destination first and discovering the time zone consequence afterwards. Invert it: decide the working hours you can sustain, then pick from the destinations that permit them.

![Remote Work travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1732808460864-b8e5eb489a52?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Connectivity: Assume Nothing

The single most common workation failure is internet that was described as "fast Wi-Fi" and is not.

- **Ask the host for a speed test screenshot** before booking anything longer than a few nights. A reputable host will send one.
- **Check upload speed, not just download.** Video calls are upload-bound, and many connections advertise a fast download over a weak upload.
- **Buy a local eSIM with a large data allowance** and test tethering on day one. This is your backup and it needs to work before you need it.
- **Identify a co-working space or a reliable café** in the first two days, before a crisis.
- **Check the power situation.** Scheduled outages are normal in parts of Asia, Africa and Latin America. A laptop with six hours of battery and a charged power bank turns an outage into an inconvenience.
- **Test your video call setup** from the actual room. Backlighting from a beautiful window makes you a silhouette.

## Where to Base Yourself

The best workation bases are not the most beautiful places. They are the places with **infrastructure**.

Look for:

- A genuine **co-working scene**, which signals reliable connectivity and a community
- **Cafés that tolerate laptops** — not universal, and in parts of Europe actively unwelcome
- A **compact centre** so errands take minutes
- **Good food that is easy to get** — cooking every meal while working full days is unsustainable
- **Something to do in the evenings and weekends** within easy reach
- A **time zone that works**

Established bases that deliver: Lisbon, Porto, Madeira, Las Palmas, Valencia, Split, Tbilisi, Chiang Mai, Bangkok, Da Nang, Hoi An, Bali's Canggu and Ubud, Mexico City, Oaxaca, Medellín, Buenos Aires, Cape Town, Goa's Assagao, and Kasol and Dharamshala in the Indian Himalaya.

## The Legal and Tax Part

Boring, and the part that causes actual problems.

**Tourist visas usually do not permit work.** In practice, remote work for a foreign employer on a tourist entry sits in a grey area that most countries do not enforce for short stays. That grey area narrows sharply as stays lengthen. For anything beyond a few weeks, look at whether the country has a digital nomad visa.

**The 183-day rule.** Spend more than roughly six months in a country in a tax year and you may become tax resident there, with obligations on your worldwide income. This is the rule that catches long-stay remote workers.

**Your employer may have a problem even if you do not.** An employee working from another country can create a taxable presence for the company, trigger local payroll obligations, or breach data-protection terms. This is why employers who seem unreasonably cautious about where you work usually are not.

**Tell your employer.** Do not quietly relocate. Many companies have a remote-work policy with a permitted country list and a maximum number of days. Asking is almost always fine. Being discovered is not.

**Check your insurance and equipment cover.** Company laptops are frequently not insured abroad, and your health insurance may not cover you outside your home country.

![Remote Work travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1673505413397-0cd0dc4f5854?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Structuring the Days

The pattern that works, repeatedly:

- **Work in blocks, not all day.** Two focused blocks with a real break between them beats eight distracted hours.
- **Do one thing outdoors before you start.** A walk, a swim, a coffee somewhere with a view. This is the entire point of being there, and if you leave it until after work you will be too tired.
- **Keep a hard finish time.** Without a commute, work expands. A fixed stop, enforced by a plan for the evening, is what stops a workation becoming just work in a hot room.
- **Protect the weekends completely.** No catching up. If you are working weekends, you have brought the worst part of your job with you.
- **Stay at least two weeks in each place.** A week is mostly setup — finding the café, the shop, the rhythm. The second week is when it starts paying off.

## The Honest Downsides

**Loneliness.** Underestimated, and the most common reason people cut trips short. Working alone in an unfamiliar city with no colleagues and no friends is isolating. Co-working spaces exist as much for this as for the desks.

**Reduced visibility at work.** Being consistently absent from the office, physical or virtual, has career consequences that nobody will tell you about directly. Over-communicate, stay on camera, and be conspicuously reliable.

**The split-attention problem.** You are in an interesting place you cannot fully explore, doing work you cannot fully focus on. Some people find this energising. Others find it a worse version of both.

**Setup cost.** Every move costs a day or two of productivity. Frequent moves mean permanent low-grade disruption. This is why slow, long stays are the sustainable pattern and two-week city-hopping is not.

## A Realistic First Attempt

Two to three weeks, one base, a time zone within three hours of home, somewhere with a co-working space and a direct flight. Tell your employer. Get an eSIM. Test the Wi-Fi on day one.

If it works, go longer next time and further afield. If it does not, you have lost very little and learned something specific about how you work.

If you are travelling with a partner or a friend who is not working the same hours — a common and underrated source of friction — agree the schedule before you go, not on day three. Putting the working blocks and the free evenings into a shared plan on **Trypinn** sounds excessive until you have spent a week negotiating every afternoon.
